questions.q: Who is LTV's Chief Financial Officer and executive sponsor for this engagement?
options: Victor Okafor
Sarah Lindqvist
Elena Marsh
Chen Liu
questions.explain: Elena Marsh is the CFO who commissions this implementation and later calls with the January 31 crisis.

questions.q: Which chapter is described as the centerpiece of this capstone?
options: Chapter 4, Wrap-Up
Chapter 1, Design and Configuration
Chapter 3, The January 31 Challenge
Chapter 2, Running the Business
questions.explain: Chapter 3 is where the CFO's January 31 call sets up the investigation and correction work that the whole capstone builds toward.

questions.q: Which supplier is configured as LTV's preferred MRO supplier with EFT payment enabled?
options: Palmetto Steel & Alloy Supply
Vantage Electrical Components Inc.
Meridian Bearing Supply Co.
Crescent Freight Logistics
questions.explain: Meridian Bearing Supply Co. is LTV's preferred MRO supplier, configured with an EFT payment method and bank account on file.

questions.q: A business unit is tied to how many primary ledgers?
options: Exactly one
Exactly two, one per currency
As many as the company has legal entities
Zero — business units are independent of ledgers
questions.explain: A business unit always references exactly one primary ledger, which is why two ledgers naturally produce two business units in this design.

questions.q: Which bank account is enabled for electronic payment file transmission, and why does this lesson flag that detail?
options: Royal Bank of Canada ...4420, because Canadian payments are always electronic
Regions Bank ...7734, because Chapter 2's supplier EFT payments go out from it and it matters again in bank reconciliation
Both accounts equally, with no particular significance
Neither account supports electronic payments in this design
questions.explain: Regions Bank's ...7734 account is enabled for EFT transmission, which matters again when Chapter 2's bank reconciliation lesson loads the January statement.

questions.q: What would FA-10452's correct January depreciation be under Manufacturing Equipment's 10-year life?
questions.explain: $145,000.00 divided by 120 months (10 years) equals $1,208.33 per month.

questions.q: Why does this lesson specifically call out PO-55210's December 22 date?
options: December 22 is LTV's fiscal year-end
It has no particular significance
Because the PO crosses a period boundary — received in December but invoiced in January, the exact shape of a GRNI accrual that resurfaces later
Because all purchase orders must be dated before December 25
questions.explain: The December-to-January timing gap is deliberately set up to create a goods-received-not-invoiced situation that matters again in lesson 17 and Chapter 3.

questions.q: Why is this problem described as different from the AP accrual or AR misapplication problems?
options: It involves a larger dollar amount than the others
It is visible immediately upon running a routine bank reconciliation, rather than hidden in a journal or invoice-level detail
It is the only problem that affects the Canadian ledger
It is the only problem caused by a system error rather than a process error
questions.explain: Unlike the GRNI accrual or the AR misapplication, which are invisible until specifically investigated, this variance shows up the moment a bank reconciliation is run — which is why Elena Marsh already knows about it.

questions.q: Why do 14 January Receivables transactions fail to generate accounting?
options: The transactions were entered with an invalid customer
Account 7850 (Freight Out) was never added to the Subledger Accounting Account Rule for that transaction type
The transactions exceeded a dollar threshold requiring manual approval
The Receivables period was already closed
questions.explain: Account 7850 was added to the chart of accounts in December, but the SLA Account Rule for the freight-charge transaction type was never updated, so Create Accounting can't find an applicable rule.

questions.q: Why is this kind of issue described as easy to miss in the moment?
options: Because the invoice amount is unusually large
Because nothing about the January invoice entry itself looks wrong — the problem only appears when viewed against a separate, earlier journal
Because Meridian is a new, untested supplier
Because the purchase order was never approved
questions.explain: Every individual step — receipt, invoice, match, validation — looks correct on its own; the issue only becomes visible when comparing against the earlier, unreversed accrual.

questions.q: Does this lesson actually correct any of the three problems it investigates?
options: Yes, all three are corrected and reconciled by the end of this lesson
No — this lesson only confirms root causes; corrections happen in lesson 21
Only the AP accrual is corrected here
Only the Harborview receipt is corrected here
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states nothing is corrected yet — all three root causes are confirmed with evidence, and fixing them is reserved for lesson 21.

questions.q: What does the Reconciliation Report specifically need to include regarding the bank variance?
options: Nothing — the bank item is omitted since it didn't require a GL fix
The bank's written confirmation that the duplicate debit was a transmission error and has been reversed
A request for LTV to switch banks
A projection of future bank fees
questions.explain: The reconciliation report ties the bank item exactly, with the bank's written confirmation of its duplicate-transmission reversal attached as evidence.

questions.q: What correction finally resolves the AP accrual problem?
options: Deleting INV-MER-88341 entirely
Increasing the supplier's payment terms to Net 60
Reclassifying the PO to a different cost center
A manual reversing journal, JE-REV-0131, debiting Accrued Liabilities and crediting Inventory clearing for $18,400.00
questions.explain: JE-REV-0131 does manually what the original auto-reverse flag should have done automatically, clearing the stale $18,400.00 accrual.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does 'the books don't balance' usually mean in a real case like this one?
options: Debits literally no longer equal credits in posted journals
Subledgers don't reconcile to the GL, reports don't tie, and known items are sitting open — not a literal debit/credit break
The chart of accounts has been deleted
The fiscal calendar has the wrong number of periods
questions.explain: Double-entry accounting doesn't silently break; the phrase really describes reconciliation and reporting gaps, not a literal imbalance in posted journals.

questions.q: What is the corrected January depreciation figure presented for FA-10452?
questions.explain: The presentation shows depreciation corrected from $2,416.67 down to the accurate $1,208.33.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend doing with the six-problem month-end crisis when discussing this project in an interview?
options: Omitting it entirely to appear more competent
Presenting it as a strength, since it demonstrates the ability to diagnose and fix real problems, not just configure correctly the first time
Blaming it entirely on other team members
Describing it only as a minor, unimportant detail
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues against hiding the crisis, framing it instead as the most interview-relevant part of the entire capstone.

questions.q: What proved that the chart of accounts' intercompany design (Requirement 2) actually worked, beyond just being configured?
options: A theoretical review with no real transactions
The fact that the unposted intercompany journal's absence was exactly what broke the close, and posting it fixed the close
A separate audit unrelated to this capstone
Running the depreciation program
questions.explain: The intercompany design was proven under real pressure: its absence (the unposted journal) directly caused a close failure, and resolving it directly fixed it.
